USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current posture — proceed with the already-announced Section 301 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports as leverage, but do not broaden the escalation further, and keep the negotiation channel open to convert China's stated willingness to increase US purchases into a concrete framework. Avoid any new tariff broadening that would deepen China's agricultural retaliation in the run-up to the 2018 midterms, while preserving the credibility that has already extracted concessions.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is moderate (threat_score +0.3), not existential: the US economy is demonstrably strong — industrial production at 103.2, consumer sentiment at 98.2, the 10-year yield near 2.98% and the broad dollar index at 112 rising (country_health), so there is no material GDP drag yet. The escalation is US-initiated and the US holds the leverage, having secured China's May 19 commitment to 'significantly increase' purchases of US goods (event_timeline 2018-05-19) and a ZTE reprieve deal on June 7. What drives the positive threat reading is real and concentrated: China's retaliatory tariffs on soybeans, aircraft and autos strike the farm belt hard — soybeans are the second-largest US export to China with ~61% of US soybean exports going there, and analysts put the hit from a 25% tariff in the billions with permanent market-share loss risk, in politically pivotal midterm districts in Iowa, North Dakota and Kansas (web_search). Add the strain on ally cohesion from the Section 232 steel/aluminum tariffs (EU, Canada, Mexico retaliation) and the risk of an escalation spiral. That is why the action is 'hold' at 0.0 rather than further escalation — broadening now would maximize farm-belt political cost and ally friction while China has already shown willingness to negotiate, and conceding outright would squander hard-won leverage. Staying the course on the announced tariffs while keeping talks open is the disciplined middle path.
